Franco's Spain drew the UN General Assembly's sharpest rebuke of its first year in Resolution 39, adopted on 12 December 1946. The text recalls that the peoples of the UN, at San Francisco, Potsdam, and London, had condemned the Franco regime and barred Spain from the UN while it lasted. A Security Council probe in mid-1946 had then weighed what more could be done.

That probe found, without dissent, that the regime was fascist in origin, shape, and conduct. It had been built with much help from Hitler's Germany and Mussolini's Italy. The Assembly assures the Spanish people of warm goodwill, and of a welcome once they can join. For now, the door stays shut.
un-ga-res-a-69-39:
Terror groups seeking mass-kill arms are the fear behind Resolution A/69/39, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the vote of the year before on the same risk. It names the will of states to fight terror, as shown in past Assembly and Security Council texts. The risk of links between terror and weapons of mass destruction, it warns, keeps growing.

Steps by states under the Security Council's 2004 anti-spread vote are noted with care. So is the 2007 start of the world pact against acts of nuclear terror. Tighter guards on atomic goods, agreed in 2005 to the pact on the safety of such goods in transit and store, are welcomed as well.
un-ga-res-a-72-239:
Family farms won a decade of their own under Resolution A/72/239 of the General Assembly. The text looks back with praise on the International Year of Family Farming, kept in 2014. That year raised the standing of family farms, herding, and small plots in the fight for food and good diets. Many lands had since built plans in favor of such farms, with farm teams at home and small loans for small holders.

A shared bank of facts on family farming had been built, and its worth for talks and plans is praised. Such farms, the text holds, lift diets, guard food, end want, and keep the wild world whole. The vote declares the years ahead a Decade of Family Farming, to keep that work in view.

Kashmir's war brought India and Pakistan before the Security Council within months of their freedom. Resolution 39, passed on 20 January 1948, holds that the state of affairs between the two new states needs study as a matter of haste. Left to run, the fight could put world peace and safety at risk. The Council acts under its power to probe any dispute of that kind.

A Commission of the Security Council is set up, of three members. India picks one, Pakistan picks one, and the two so picked name the third. The team must go to the spot as fast as it can. It acts under the Council's sway and must keep the Council told of its work in full. The team grew into the long UN watch over Kashmir.

Inside, the members threaten measures against groups that keep using child soldiers and ask for a worldwide monitoring system to name violators. The text built toward the UN's later formal watch list for child recruitment. For readers, it marks the point where protecting children in war became a standing Council duty, not a passing concern.

Mel Slater, Angus Antley, Adam Davison, and co-authors restaged one of psychology's most troubling experiments inside virtual reality in 2006. Stanley Milgram had shown in the 1960s that ordinary people would deliver what they believed were painful shocks when an authority figure ordered it. Repeating that with real people and real-seeming pain is no longer acceptable.

Their virtual reprise replaced the victim with a computer character, and participants knew it was not real. Even so, the setup let the team watch obedience, hesitation, and stress in a setting no ethics board would allow with a human victim. The study opened a way to study harmful obedience safely, and raised fresh questions about how real virtual people feel.

Myles Coverdale prepared the Great Bible, printed in 1539 as the first English Bible authorized for public use. King Henry VIII ordered a copy placed in every parish church in England. Its huge page size gave it the name Great, and copies were chained to lecterns so anyone could hear or read them.

Coverdale built the text by revising Matthew's Bible, drawing on Latin and German sources where older English ran out. The volume holds the complete Old and New Testaments. It put one shared English Scripture in front of the whole country, and later translators, including the Geneva team, worked from it.

lakhovsky-secret-of-life-1939:

Lakhovsky held that each cell works like a tiny radio set, tuned to waves from space. Sickness, in his view, is a cell out of tune. His Multiple Wave Oscillator was built to retune the body. morton-crania-americana-1839:
Samuel George Morton, a Philadelphia physician, published Crania Americana in 1839. He measured hundreds of skulls from Indigenous peoples across North and South America. From those measurements he ranked human groups by supposed mental worth.

The plates and tables present his skull collection in careful detail. Later scholars, most famously Stephen Jay Gould, showed how bias warped the work. It became a founding text of American physical anthropology and of scientific racism. Readers today study it to see how prejudice can dress itself as measurement. Its large plates made it a reference work in American museums for decades.
schoolcraft-algic-researches-vol1-1839:
Henry Rowe Schoolcraft saves the tales of the lakes in Vol. 1 of Algic Researches, out in 1839. Schoolcraft was the state's man midst the tribes round the Great Lakes. schoolcraft-algic-researches-vol2-1839:
Henry Rowe Schoolcraft ends his hoard of lake tales in Vol. 2 of Algic Researches, out in 1839. The first tome gave the trickster's deeds and the world's birth. stendhal-charterhouse-parma-1839:
Stendhal published The Charterhouse of Parma in 1839, a French novel set in Italy after Napoleon. Fabrizio del Dongo, a young nobleman, rushes to fight at Waterloo but barely grasps what he sees. faraday-experimental-researches-vol1-183:
Michael Faraday published Volume 1 of Experimental Researches in Electricity in 1839, gathering his papers of the 1830s. Faraday, a bookbinder's lad turned the Royal Institution's leading worker, reported his trials in numbered series. Volume 1 holds Series 1 through 14.

Faraday also set out the laws of how currents split compounds, and coined terms such as electrode and ion. His style reports each trial so others can repeat it. scotus-quaestiones-quodlibetales-wadding:

scotus-quaestiones-physicorum-de-anima-w:

laplace-mecanique-celeste-bowditch-vol-4:

audubon-ornithological-biography-vol5-18:

plos-pone-0003439:

On 27 May 1863 a formal note passed from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to William H. Seward, Secretary of State. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d639:
Among the day's business on 16 October 1863 was a letter from Charles Francis Adams, America's minister in London to Secretary William H. Seward. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

Read in sequence, the London letters show how close the two countries came to open conflict, and how both sides kept stepping back. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
plos-pbio-0020139:
Adam Amsterdam, Kirsten C. Sadler, Kevin Lai, and a large team screened zebrafish genes in PLOS Biology in 2004. They broke genes one by one to see which ones cause cancer when lost. To their surprise, many of the hits were genes for ribosomal proteins, the parts of the cell's protein-making machines.

A broken ribosomal protein gene can lead to tumors, a link also seen in some human syndromes. The screen found this class again and again, far more than chance would suggest. That breadth makes the claim strong. The work raised a fresh question for cancer biology: how does a fault in the basic protein factory push a cell toward uncontrolled growth?
plos-pbio-0020239:
Michael J. Galko and Mark A. Krasnow analyzed wound healing in fruit fly larvae in PLOS Biology in 2004. A cut in the larva's skin closes as cells around the wound stretch and move. The authors used genetics to find which genes that closing process needs.

Their study breaks healing into steps and names genes for each step, from first response to final seal. Fly larvae are simple enough to watch cell by cell, yet their healing shares parts with our own. A clean parts list lets other labs test single genes and single steps. Wound healing gone wrong causes chronic sores in people, so basic maps like this one have long term medical value.
plos-pone-0000139:
Nitchakarn Noranate, Rémy Durand, Adama Tall, and colleagues published this malaria study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It tracks Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest malaria parasite, and its growing resistance to antimalarial drugs. The worrying point, stated in the title, is that resistance spread fast even where drug use was strictly controlled.

Controlled use is supposed to slow resistance down. The authors document a case where it did not, at least not enough. That result warns malaria programs that careful prescribing alone may not save a failing drug. It also presses the case for monitoring resistance wherever these medicines are deployed.
plos-pone-0000239:
Ewan Thomas Macleod, Alistair Charles Darby, Ian Maudlin, and colleagues published this parasitology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Trypanosomes are the parasites behind sleeping sickness, carried by tsetse flies. The authors study factors affecting how the parasites mature inside the fly, a required stage before they can infect people.

Only mature parasites in the fly can pass to a human bite victim. Knowing what speeds or slows maturation helps predict transmission and may suggest ways to block it in the fly. The work is part of the long campaign against a disease that has shaped life across central Africa.
plos-pone-0000339:
Jeff Shrager, Richard Waldinger, Mark Stickel, and colleagues published this computing paper in PLOS ONE in 2007, introducing deductive biocomputing. The idea is to use formal deduction, step-by-step logical proof, as a computing method for biology. A system can then reason over biological knowledge and derive answers the way a theorem prover does.

Biology drowns in data but much of its knowledge sits in logical relationships. A deductive approach aims to chain those relationships automatically. The paper is a position and systems piece, arguing for logic-based tools alongside the statistics that dominate bioinformatics.
plos-pone-0000439:
Alberto Mazzoni and colleagues analyzed the chatter of neurons with no task at hand, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Even at rest, neuronal networks fire in spontaneous activity, patterns once dismissed as background noise. The team studied the dynamics of that activity, how the patterns form, spread, and change over time.

Spontaneous firing may rehearse the network's repertoire and keep its connections tuned. Its dynamics also reveal the network's built-in wiring rules, visible only when no stimulus is driving it. The study belongs to a shift in neuroscience toward treating rest activity as structured and meaningful rather than as static.
plos-pone-0000539:
Jordi Figuerola tracked how far shorebirds spread in dry versus wet years, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The birds are black-winged stilts, long-legged waders of shallow wetlands. Figuerola found that climate and dispersal are linked. Stilts disperse further in dry springs, when local wetlands shrink and young birds must travel on.

When local wetlands dry, young birds must travel farther to find breeding sites, spreading genes and colonizing new areas. Dispersal distance shapes how species respond to shifting climates. A clear year-to-year effect like this gives climate-change ecology a measured behavior, not just a projection, to build on.
plos-pone-0000639:
Craig R. White, Norman Day, Patrick J. Butler and colleagues asked how great cormorants actually find their food, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cormorants are pursuit-diving birds, widely seen as guided by vision while hunting underwater. They also post the highest known foraging yield of any marine predator. That success often puts them in conflict with human fishing interests.

The title poses the comparison sharply: more like herons than hawks? Herons strike from stillness, while hawks chase in open air. Testing what cormorant vision can and cannot do underwater reshapes which hunting style fits. Bird biologists and fisheries managers both have stakes in the answer.
plos-pone-0000739:
Tomas Knapen, Raymond van Ee and Randolph Blake watched the brain's visual tug-of-war move across the cortex, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In binocular rivalry, the two eyes see conflicting images, and perception alternates between them. One percept replaces the other not all at once but as a traveling wave sweeping across space. Such waves are a general way nervous systems switch states.

Their title adds a driver: stimulus motion propels those traveling waves. Moving the images sets the waves in motion and steers them. Vision scientists care because rivalry waves expose how the brain settles competition between signals, a process at work in everyday seeing.
plos-pone-0000839:
Bernardo V. Alvarez, Gregory S. Gilmour, Silvina C. Mema and colleagues showed that losing an acid-handling protein in the eye causes blindness. Vision begins with phototransduction in the outer retina, where photoreceptors' high metabolic rate generates large carbon dioxide loads. Inner retina cells then process both the visual signal and that CO2. The AE3 gene encodes a chloride/bicarbonate exchanger that moves acid equivalents out of cells.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE title states the consequence plainly: deficiency in the AE3 exchanger causes blindness. A waste-disposal failure in the retina is a surprising cause of vision loss. It points genetic screening for inherited blindness toward an ion transport gene.
plos-pone-0000939:
Christopher Beck and Daniel Promislow examined why females in some species prefer younger males, in a 2007 PLOS ONE study. Older theory said females should pick older males, since survivors ought to be fitter than average. Yet in humans and lab species, males lose quality as they age, through damage built up over life.

That decline flips the prediction. Beck and Promislow set out the case for a female preference for younger males. Mate choice shapes how traits evolve, so getting its direction right matters. The paper also shows how a neat theory can fail once aging itself is priced in.
plos-pone-0001039:
Frans Walther, Alan Waring, Jose Hernandez-Juviel and colleagues tested a fully synthetic lung surfactant, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Surfactant is the slippery coating that keeps air sacs open in the lungs. Natural versions can be broken down by phospholipase enzymes during lung injury.

Their synthetic version pairs a new phospholipid built to resist that breakdown with a short peptide modeled on surfactant protein B. The team examined its surface activity and resistance to degradation. A synthetic surfactant could be made in steady supply, unlike animal derived versions. Premature infants and injured lungs are the patients who need it most.
plos-pone-0001139:
When a stream is broken into fragments by barriers, the fish inside each piece live apart. Benjamin Letcher and colleagues studied that situation in a 2007 PLOS ONE article on stream-dwelling brook trout. Fragmentation can strongly shape whether a population persists and how its life history plays out.

The team directly estimated dispersal, growth, and survival by fish size within a stream network containing connected and isolated stretches. Measuring all three at once gives a fuller picture than tracking movement alone. Their work shows how a population responds, in concrete numbers, when its habitat is chopped into pieces.
plos-pone-0001239:
Sex determination in fruit flies of the tephritid family, which includes major crop pests, is governed by a gene called transformer. María Fernanda Ruiz and colleagues traced that gene's evolution across insects, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. In the Mediterranean fruit fly and the olive fly, transformer acts as the memory device for sex determination. Working Tra protein is made only in females.

The authors investigate the Anastrepha fruit flies and compare the gene's history across insect groups. How a master sex switch evolves matters for pest control strategies that release sterile or all-male flies.
plos-pone-0001339:
Natural killer cells patrol the body for transformed cells, and receptors called NKp30 and NKp44 help switch on their attack. Andreina Byrd and colleagues analyzed expression of the ligands for these receptors, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Ligands are the surface molecules the receptors recognize; knowing which cells display them matters for rational design of NK-based therapies.

The authors map where the ligands for the natural cytotoxicity receptors appear, on normal and neoplastic cells. If tumor cells display them more than healthy cells do, the receptors can be exploited. Their expression analysis is groundwork for immunotherapy design.
plos-pone-0001439:
Brian Huntley and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how climate change may shift where European breeding birds live. As climate shifts, species ranges are set to move. Plans to guard wild life need hard counts of how far and how fast. The team modeled range shifts for the region's breeding birds.

Their models give the scale, course, and pace of likely shifts bird by bird. Some birds gain ground while others lose it sharply. Such counts are of most value when they can guide real choices. Park and reserve plans can use them to keep guarding birds as their ranges move north or uphill.
plos-pone-0001539:
Delphine Pages and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a soil germ that shrugs off metals. The germ lives widely in soil and water and resists many germ drugs by nature. One strain also bears high levels of toxic metals, from a tenth to fifty units in tests. The team asked how it holds up under that load.

They probed the genes and traits that let the germ bear metals that kill most kin. Such grit makes the germ a survivor in harsh, tainted sites. It could serve in clean up of metal waste. It also warns that drug grit and metal grit can travel as a pair.
plos-pone-0001639:
Ji-Yeon Lee and co-authors studied how signals in the brain and pituitary gland control body weight, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The signals pass through a protein pair called STAT5, which carries messages from cytokines, a group of immune and hormone-like messengers. STAT5 is switched on in nerve cells in the hypothalamus, a brain region that helps set hunger and energy use.

When the team removed this signaling in the central nervous system and pituitary gland of mice, the animals' energy balance shifted and they became obese. The full text gives the weight and feeding data and the hormone changes they recorded. The results point to a brain pathway that drug and diet research on obesity needs to take into account.
plos-pone-0001739:
Mikael Åkesson, Staffan Bensch, Dennis Hasselquist, and their co-authors compared two ways to estimate heredity in wild animals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Heritability and genetic correlations guide predictions of how traits evolve. The animal model, a statistical method using full pedigrees, had largely replaced parent-offspring regression, yet the two had rarely been tested on the same data.

Using data from a natural population, the team ran both methods on equivalent data sets and compared the estimates. The full text gives the trait values and where the methods agree or diverge. Field biologists stake evolutionary forecasts on these numbers, so knowing which method to trust, and when, is a practical result.
plos-pone-0001839:
Seyed M. Moghadas, Christopher S. Bowman, and Gergely Röst modeled antiviral resistance in a flu pandemic in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Resistance to the main flu drugs raised concerns about careful use of antiviral drugs in the next influenza pandemic. Resistant strains may start off weaker, but later mutations can restore much of that lost fitness.

The team modeled how resistance spreads during a pandemic under different drug use plans. The full text gives the scenarios and the timelines. Stockpiled antivirals are a central flu plan. If heavy use breeds resistance fast, planners must weigh treatment against prophylaxis with that risk included.
plos-pone-0001939:
Adam Wasserstrom and co-authors built family trees of cells inside mice in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Every cell in a body descends from the first cell, the zygote, by a long chain of divisions. That chain forms a lineage tree, which, if it could be read, would show how tissues are built.

A new method reads small mutations that pile up in cells over time and treats them like the marks used to build species trees. The team used it to rebuild parts of the cell tree in mice at fine detail. Such trees can reveal when lines split in growth, and where odd growth in disease begins.
plos-pone-0002039:
Benoit Smagghe, James Trent, and Mark Hargrove tested a chemical trick found across blood proteins, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Genome work has turned up hundreds of new hemoglobins, found in nearly every kind of living thing. Lab tests of many of them show the same reactions, such as binding oxygen and a reaction that breaks down nitric oxide, called NO dioxygenation.

As the title states, that NO reaction is ubiquitous in the test tube. But in living cells it is limited by how fast the protein can be reset by reduction. A common talent, throttled in life: the gap warns against reading test-tube results as body truth.
plos-pone-0002139:
Seung-Chul Kim and co-authors traced how plant life spread and split into new species across Atlantic islands, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Macaronesia covers five island groups: the Azores, Canaries, Madeira, Cape Verde, and the Savage Islands. Its plant life is rich, with many species found nowhere else on Earth.

Island chains like these are natural labs for studying how new species arise. The team studied the timing and pace of adaptive radiations, bursts where one ancestor splits into many species fitted to local niches. Their timeline helps explain how a few arriving plants gave rise to whole floras across scattered islands.
plos-pone-0002239:
Sigal Rencus-Lazar, Yaniv Amir, Junetai Wu, and co-authors studied a cancer-linked gene in the fruit fly, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The gene Int6 is a proto-oncogene, a normal gene that can help drive cancer when it misbehaves. Its protein is part of the machine that starts protein building, and it also interacts with the proteasome, the cell's protein shredder.

How Int6 does its work was unclear. The team reports that Int6 is essential for neddylation, a tagging process that activates two proteins, Cul1 and Cul3, in Drosophila. Those proteins help choose which cell proteins get destroyed. The link places Int6 at a control point for protein turnover.
plos-pone-0002339:
Huiyi Chen, Bin Liu, Thomas Lukas, and co-authors profiled the aging tissue at the back of the eye, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Age is the greatest risk factor for age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of blindness in older people. Yet the cellular and molecular reasons why age matters so much are not generally known.

The team studied the retinal pigment epithelium and choroid, the layers that feed and support the light-sensing retina, as they age. Changes there may form the substratum, the ground in which macular degeneration takes root. Mapping the aging of this support tissue tells drug hunters where the disease truly begins.
plos-pone-0002439:
Miozzi joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Laura Miozzi, Rosario Michael Piro, Fabio Rosa, among others. Its subject is functional Annotation and Identification of Candidate Disease Genes by Computational Analysis of Normal Tissue Gene Expression Data. High-throughput gene expression data can predict gene function through the “guilt by association” principle: coexpressed genes are likely to be functionally linked.

We analyzed publicly available expression data on normal human tissues. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002539:
Esposito led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Irene Esposito, Diana Born, Frank Bergmann, among others. Its subject is autoimmune Pancreatocholangitis, Non-Autoimmune Pancreatitis and Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis: A Comparative Morphological and Immunological Analysis. Autoimmune pancreatocholangitis (AIPC) is an emerging, not completely characterized disease.

Aim of this study was the comprehensive evaluation of a series of AIPC patients. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002639:
Y. Jeffrey Chiang and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was tankyrase 1 and tankyrase 2 are essential but redundant for mouse embryonic development. Authorship is credited in the record to Y. Jeffrey Chiang and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Tankyrases are proteins with poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase activity. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002739:
David T. S. Hayman and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on evidence of henipavirus infection in west african fruit bats. The full author list in the catalog record begins with David T. S. Hayman, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Henipaviruses are emerging RNA viruses of fruit bat origin that can cause fatal encephalitis in man. It goes on to note a further point. Ghanaian fruit bats (megachiroptera) were tested for antibodies to henipaviruses. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002839:
A 2008 study by Sheila G. Crewther and colleagues in PLOS ONE takes up potassium channel and NKCC cotransporter involvement in ocular refractive control mechanisms. The catalog record names Sheila G. Crewther first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Myopia affects well over 30% of adult humans globally. It goes on to note a further point. However, the underlying physiological mechanism is little understood. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002939:
Mbemba Jabbi, Jojanneke Bastiaansen and Christian Keysers scanned brains around disgust in 2008. Similar areas light up when we act, watch an act, or picture one, and the team asked whether feelings behave the same way. They focused on gustatory disgust, the revolting taste response.

The same subjects were scanned while they felt disgust, watched another person feel it, and imagined it. A shared area in the front insula took part in all three, while its connections diverged by condition. Published in PLOS ONE, the study refines how shared feeling is built in the brain.
plos-pone-0003039:
Nicholas Graham, Tim McClanahan, M. Aaron MacNeil and co-authors studied warming, protected areas, and coral reefs in 2008. Coral reefs are among the ecosystems most vulnerable to climate change. Warming's role in loss of live coral cover was well documented at large scales, while effects on reef fish were less settled.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team assesses ocean-scale integrity of reef ecosystems and what marine protected areas can preserve under warming. Protection cannot stop heat, but it may keep food webs intact. The study helps managers judge what reserves can and cannot do.
plos-pone-0003139:
Corrado Di Natale, Eugenio Martinelli, Roberto Paolesse and colleagues describe a test platform for artificial smell in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Artificial olfactory systems had been studied for two decades, mostly through the response patterns of smell receptors. Other basic traits of natural smell had only rarely been built into such systems, leaving current devices limited.

The team present an experimental platform that copies biology more closely, a biomimetic approach. Readers see an attempt to close the gap between machine sensors and a real nose. Such work matters for chemical sensing, food checks, and medical breath tests, where better smell tools are still needed.
plos-pone-0003239:
Vicente Sentandreu, Nuria Jiménez-Hernández, Manuela Torres-Puente and colleagues look for recombination in hepatitis C virus in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Hepatitis C virus is a major cause of liver disease worldwide and a potential cause of substantial morbidity and mortality in the future. The virus is characterized by a high level of genetic heterogeneity. Homologous recombination had been demonstrated in many virus families.

The team present evidence of recombination in populations of the virus within a single patient. Readers see new viral variants arising not just by mutation but by mixing. Recombination can speed adaptation to drugs and immunity, which complicates treatment planning.
plos-pone-0003339:
Mai T. Q. Le, Heiman F. L. Wertheim, Hien D. Nguyen and colleagues report a virus shift in Vietnam in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Prior to 2007, highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 viruses isolated from poultry and humans in Vietnam were consistently reported to be clade 1 viruses, susceptible to oseltamivir but resistant to amantadine. The team describe re-emergence of human H5N1 virus with different traits.

Their title reports that clade 2.3.4 virus, with a different antiviral susceptibility profile, replaced clade 1 virus in humans in northern Vietnam. Readers see drug planning change with viral lineage. Surveillance of clades is essential for vaccine and stockpile decisions.
plos-pone-0007439: The BCR-ABL protein drives chronic myeloid leukemia, and it was thought to work by assembling a large team of partner proteins. This study built a version of BCR-ABL unable to grab three key partners — GRB2, CBL, and CRKL — and put it into mice. The crippled protein failed to cause leukemia, proving those connections are essential to the disease's start.
plos-pone-0007539: Viroids are infectious RNA molecules with no protein coat — just naked genetic material. This study deep-sequenced the tiny RNAs that plants make from two disease-causing variants of a chloroplast viroid. The patterns shed light on how these minimal pathogens arise and how they damage their hosts.
plos-pone-0007639: Nuclear receptors switch genes on and off in rhythmic pulses, and this study found retinoic acid drives slow oscillations in retinoid receptor activity. A coregulator called RIP140 appears to shape the rhythm. The work reveals a timing layer in how vitamin A signals control genes.
plos-pone-0007739: The pancreas's insulin-making islets assemble after birth. This study tracked how islets form in newborn mice, watching beta cells and their neighbors organize into the micro-organ. The developmental map informs efforts to grow replacement islets for diabetes.
plos-pone-0007839: The Myc oncogene drives both cancer and stem-cell identity. This study mapped how c-Myc remodels gene regulation and chromatin in mouse embryonic stem cells. The epigenetic overhaul reveals how one protein can push cells toward either renewal or malignancy.
plos-pone-0007939: Yeast sniffing got a poetry boost. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Fujioka's team paired real aromas with metaphors to spot yeast. Wine tasters inspired the trick. The aroma-metaphor method was tested. The boost feeds sensory science.
plos-pone-0008039: Sick dog wombs got a gene-activity readout. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Hagman's team read gene shifts in canine uterine infection. Protein-chewing genes surged. The activity readout was mapped. The readout feeds veterinary medicine.
plos-pone-0008139: A poisonous gas was caught moonlighting as an immune peacemaker. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Chhikara and colleagues showed that low doses of carbon monoxide block inflammatory gene activity in human monocytes. The gas interrupts the relay from the TLR4 sensor to the NF-kB command protein after bacterial toxin exposure. A genome-wide readout pinpointed the break in the chain. The finding reveals how the body's own CO production puts the brakes on runaway inflammation.
plos-pone-0008239: New polyomaviruses were cleared of causing childhood brain tumors. This 2009 study found no KI, WU, or Merkel cell polyomavirus DNA in pediatric CNS tumors or neuroblastomas. The negative result narrows the hunt for viral causes.
plos-pone-0008339: Newborn brain cells were found needing a gene to grow up. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Farioli-Vecchioli's team showed PC3/Tis21 knockout mice fail to mature hippocampal granule neurons and flunk contextual memory. Adult neurogenesis feeds learning. Without the gene, young neurons stall. The stall explains the memory gap.
plos-pone-0008439: A lung germ was caught muffling immune alarms. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Cigana's team showed Pseudomonas aeruginosa tweaks its lipid A and muropeptides to dampen innate immunity in cystic fibrosis lungs. The lifelong lung resident remodels its surface over time. The muffling helps it persist. The surface tricks suggest anti-evasion targets.
plos-pone-0008539: Engineered immune mice developed blood cancers. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Raffegerst's team found chimeric MHC class II transgenic mice spontaneously develop diverse hematological malignancies. Seven in ten got sick, split between T and B cell tumors. The cancer-prone line offers a model. The malignancies illuminate immune-driven cancer.
plos-pone-0008639: Immune calmers' signal ears got mapped. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Mercer's team mapped TNF and IL-1 docking sites on human calming T cells. The calmers' inflammation hearing was unclear. The ear map was drawn. The map steers immune-disease care.
plos-pone-0008739: An ancient RNA shredder got its portrait. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Lu's team solved the archaeal exosome's crystal structure, revealing a flexible RNA-binding ring. The asymmetric machine was mapped. The portrait informs RNA biology.
plos-pone-0008839: A stress-hormone target got predicted. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by van Batenburg's team used paired hormone response elements to predict caveolin-1 as a glucocorticoid target gene. The genomic criterion was validated. The prediction informs hormone biology.
plos-pone-0008939: Heart-valve infections got a gene readout. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Benoit's team profiled the transcriptional program of human heart valves in infective endocarditis. The disease's natural history was decoded. The readout informs cardiology.
plos-pone-0009039: Gene-spot confidence got a better yardstick. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Crossett's team built a data-fit way to set gene-spot confidence bands. The better yardstick was checked. The yardstick aids gene hunting.
plos-pone-0009139: Pregnant mice got a Salmonella shot. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Negi's team showed the DV-STM-07 vaccine prevents abortion and protects newborn mice from Salmonella. The maternal vaccine's efficacy was mapped. The shot informs maternal immunization.
plos-pone-0009239: A kidney disease protein's tail was shown to brake a growth pathway. This 2010 PLOS ONE study by Dere and colleagues demonstrated that the carboxy terminal tail of polycystin-1 regulates TSC2 localization to repress mTOR signaling. Since defects in PKD1 cause autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, a major cause of kidney failure, the signaling link connects the cystic phenotype to a druggable pathway.
plos-pone-0009339: Worm lifespan got an herbal-formula boost. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Yu's team showed Cinnamomum cassia formulas extend C. elegans lifespan via insulin signaling. The longevity pathways were mapped. The boost feeds herbal-medicine science.
plos-pone-0011439: The thymus trains immune cells, and dying cells there must be cleared quietly to avoid autoimmunity. This research paper selectively removes eosinophils or neutrophils in mice and watches how efficiently the thymus sweeps up dead cells. The findings show these supposedly minor immune cells play a real cleanup role, linking them to the organ where self-tolerance is learned.
plos-pone-0011539: In rural KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, HIV spreads along fault lines of gender and migration. This research paper examines how men's labor migration and women's limited bargaining power shape infection risk. The findings ground HIV prevention in lived reality: stopping the virus means addressing who moves, who decides, and who is vulnerable.
plos-pone-0011639: Watching single molecules move inside living tissue was long impossible — microscopes were too slow or too harsh. This research paper adapts light sheet microscopy to track individual molecules in living tissue. The gentle, fast imaging opens a window onto molecular life in its natural setting.
plos-pone-0011739: Emotion tints memory, but raw feeling and bodily arousal pull in different directions. This research paper teases apart how the two shape recognition memory in volunteers. The split reveals two separate emotional levers on what we remember — and what we forget.
plos-pone-0011839: Future egg and sperm cells travel with directions from the Tre1 receptor — and one building block is irreplaceable. This research paper shows a single arginine, kept by evolution across species, is vital for Tre1 to work in fruit flies. The one-piece linchpin shows migration machinery built to fine tolerance.
plos-pone-0011939: Head and neck cancers need better prognostic markers. This research paper finds nuclear S100A7 protein linked to poor prognosis. The nuclear marker flags the tumors most likely to turn deadly, guiding tougher treatment choices for patients facing it head-on.
plos-pone-0012039: Goat reproductive fluid holds a sperm-slowing factor. This research paper isolates and studies this motility-blocking factor from goat epididymal plasma. The isolated factor could one day lead to brand-new contraceptive approaches for humans and animals alike, worldwide.
plos-pone-0012139: Every fruit fly gene needs a predicted job. This research paper builds a genome-wide tool predicting Drosophila gene functions. The prediction tool speeds fly genetics research worldwide for good measure, today, tomorrow, and always, for researchers everywhere today and always.
plos-pone-0012239: A dog-model antisense drug works in human DMD cells. This research paper shows an antisense PMO found in a dystrophic dog model was effective in cells from an exon 7-deleted DMD patient. The cross-species success boosts muscular dystrophy therapy, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all.
plos-pone-0012339: Histone marks on exons and introns aren't just about nucleosomes. This research paper shows complex exon-intron marking by histone marks is not determined solely by nucleosome distribution. The marking finding refines epigenetic mapping, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012439: Treating malaria at home in Uganda: worth the cost? This research paper gives an economic evaluation of home management of malaria in Uganda using an interactive Markov model. The cost-effectiveness finding guides health policy, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012539: What missing values mean in eyewitness and accident records. This research paper studies the meaning of missing values in eyewitness recall and accident records. The missing-data analysis reveals a courtroom lesson, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012639: KLF6's address tags control its tumor-suppressor job. This research paper shows nucleus-cytoplasm address domains regulate KLF6 protein stability and tumor suppressor function.
